question.problem:
Given that $f(x)={x}^{2}$, the instantaneous rate of change ${f}^{′}(-1)$ can be computed using the limit of a difference quotient. The first few steps of this calculation are shown below:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & =…\end{aligned}
$$

Finish the calculation, and hence find ${f}^{′}(-1).$
question.worked_solution:
By proceeding with the remaining calculations we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{(-1+h)^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{1-2h+{h}^{2}-1}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}\frac{h(-2+h)}{h} \\  & ={lim}_{h\to 0}(-2+h) \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{′}(-1)=-2.$
